body:
Cinema as a Performing Art and Mass Medium

Cinema combines acting, storytelling, literature, music, dance and visual expression. Unlike traditional theatre, which depends on a live performance before an audience, cinema presents recorded performances that can be shown repeatedly to audiences in different places.

This ability to reach large audiences makes cinema an important medium of mass communication. In India, cinema developed into a powerful means of entertainment, cultural expression, social education and the communication of national and regional identities.

Introduction of Cinema in India

The first public exhibition of motion pictures in India took place on 7 July 1896 at Watson's Hotel in Bombay, now Mumbai. The films were associated with the Lumiere brothers of France and were exhibited by their representative, Marius Sestier.

This event introduced Indian audiences to cinema. However, the exhibition of foreign films must be distinguished from the subsequent production of Indian feature films.

Raja Harishchandra: Beginning of Indian Feature Cinema

Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, popularly known as Dadasaheb Phalke, directed Raja Harishchandra in 1913. It is conventionally recognised as India's first full-length indigenous feature film.

The film was based on the traditional story of King Harishchandra, who remained committed to truth despite severe personal suffering. Its public commercial exhibition began on 3 May 1913 in Bombay.

It was a silent film, meaning that it did not contain synchronised recorded dialogue. Its success demonstrated that Indian stories, traditions and cultural values could attract audiences through the new medium.

Dadasaheb Phalke is consequently remembered as the Father of Indian Cinema.

Alam Ara: Beginning of the Sound Era

Alam Ara, directed by Ardeshir Irani, was released on 14 March 1931 at the Majestic Cinema in Bombay. It was India's first talking feature film, commonly called the first Indian talkie.

The introduction of recorded dialogue and songs transformed Indian cinema. Language became a central feature of films, encouraging the development of distinct film industries in Gujarati, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu and other Indian languages.

Ardeshir Irani was also the producer of Kisan Kanya (1937), directed by Moti B. Gidwani, which is recognised as India's first indigenously produced colour feature film.

Bombay as a Centre of Indian Cinema

By 1925, Bombay had emerged as a major centre of Indian filmmaking. Artists, writers and performers migrated there from different regions, including Lahore, Calcutta and Madras. Their participation gave the film industry a broadly national character.

Bombay's films also portrayed the opportunities, poverty and difficulties experienced by people migrating to large cities. Cinema thus became a record of changing Indian social life as well as a source of entertainment.

Prelims focus

  • First public film exhibition in India: Bombay, 7 July 1896.
  • Raja Harishchandra, 1913: Dadasaheb Phalke; silent feature film.
  • Alam Ara, 1931: Ardeshir Irani; first Indian talkie.
  • Kisan Kanya, 1937: first indigenously produced Indian colour feature film.
  • Trap: Dadasaheb Phalke directed the pioneering silent feature, whereas Ardeshir Irani directed the first Indian talkie.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Work, Life and Leisure, section 4.5, pp. 145-146; National Film Archive of India, Special Screening of Rare Footage at NFAI, 2017; Press Information Bureau, National Film Awards factsheet, 20 September 2026; Kerala higher secondary Journalism textbook, Film Appreciation; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Kisan Kanya. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Origin and Early Milestones of Indian Cinema

body:
Theatre as a Composite Performing Art

Theatre communicates stories and ideas through live dramatic performances. Indian theatre traditions combine dialogue, acting, music, dance and storytelling. They draw upon mythology, religious narratives, historical events, literature and everyday social experiences.

The classical foundations of Indian dramatic art are associated with the Natya Shastra, traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni. Alongside classical drama, different regions developed their own folk theatre traditions in local languages.

These traditions provided early Indian cinema with experienced performers, familiar stories, dramatic conventions and established musical traditions.

Bhavai: The Folk Theatre of Gujarat

Bhavai is a traditional form of Gujarati folk theatre. Its origin is conventionally associated with Asait Thakar, also written as Asait Thakore, of Unjha in the 14th century.

Bhavai developed in association with religious traditions, particularly the worship of Goddess Amba, and subsequently became an important form of popular entertainment and social commentary.

Individual dramatic episodes of Bhavai are known as Vesha. Performances commonly use humour, dialogue and satire to portray the behaviour of different social groups and expose social evils.

Bhavai is significant not merely because it preserves Gujarati folklore but also because it provides a means of questioning social inequalities and harmful customs. Its influence is particularly visible in Ketan Mehta's Gujarati film Bhavni Bhavai (1980), which addresses caste discrimination and untouchability.

Major Regional Folk Theatre Traditions

Theatre traditionPrincipal regional association
BhavaiGujarat
NautankiUttar Pradesh
TamashaMaharashtra
JatraBengal and eastern India
YakshaganaKarnataka

These are principal regional associations rather than exclusive geographical boundaries. Folk theatre traditions can spread beyond their regions of origin.

Parsi Theatre and Early Indian Cinema

Parsi theatre developed into a popular commercial theatre tradition during the 19th century, particularly in Bombay. Its touring companies presented historical, mythological, romantic and social dramas in languages understood by diverse audiences.

Its mixture of dramatic storytelling, music and popular entertainment influenced early Indian films. The transition from stage to cinema allowed stories previously performed before local audiences to reach much wider audiences.

Indian People's Theatre Association

The Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA) was established in 1943. It used theatre, songs and other performing arts to raise awareness of poverty, exploitation, famine and other social problems.

IPTA was associated with progressive cultural movements during the later phase of the freedom struggle. Its influence extended to socially conscious Indian cinema.

Dharti Ke Lal (1946), directed by Khwaja Ahmad Abbas, was an IPTA film dealing with the Bengal famine of 1943 and the suffering of ordinary people.

Prelims focus

  • Natya Shastra: traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni.
  • Bhavai: Gujarati folk theatre associated with Asait Thakar.
  • Vesha: an individual dramatic episode of Bhavai.
  • Parsi theatre: important influence on early popular Indian cinema.
  • IPTA: established in 1943; associated with socially conscious performing arts.
  • Dharti Ke Lal: K. A. Abbas; Bengal famine.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 10, Theatre Crafts, pp. 112-123, particularly p. 113; CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Class 11, Module 10, Theatre and Drama in India, Bhavai section; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Parsi Rangbhumi and Bhavai; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, historical material on IPTA and Dharti Ke Lal. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Indian Theatre Traditions and Their Connection with Cinema

body:
The Gujarati Contribution to Early Indian Cinema

Gujarati entrepreneurs, writers, actors and filmmakers participated in Indian cinema during the silent-film period. Bombay's proximity to Gujarat and its established Gujarati commercial and cultural communities encouraged this participation.

However, a silent film made by a Gujarati filmmaker should not automatically be classified as a Gujarati-language talkie. Gujarati-language cinema acquired a clearer linguistic identity after the introduction of sound.

Narsinh Mehta: The First Gujarati Talkie

Narsinh Mehta, released in 1932, was the first Gujarati talking feature film. It was directed by Nanubhai Vakil and produced by Sagar Movietone.

The film portrayed the life of the celebrated Gujarati Bhakti saint and poet Narsinh Mehta. Its subject connected the emerging Gujarati film industry with the state's devotional literature, religious traditions and ideals of social equality.

Indian and Gujarati sound-film milestones

Alam Ara (1931) was the first Indian talkie, while Narsinh Mehta (1932) was the first Gujarati talkie. They belong to different linguistic milestones.

Gujarati Literature and Rural Society in Cinema

Gujarati cinema developed a close relationship with regional literature. Filmmakers adapted novels, short stories, legends and plays, bringing literary narratives to audiences who might not otherwise encounter the original written works.

Liludi Dharati (1968)

Liludi Dharati, directed by Vallabh Choksi, is conventionally recognised as the first Gujarati colour feature film. It was adapted from the novel of the same name by Chunilal Madia.

The film depicts rural life and agrarian society. It represents the connection between Gujarati literature and regional filmmaking.

Kanku (1969)

Kanku, directed by Kantilal Rathod, was based on a literary work by Pannalal Patel. Set in rural northern Gujarat, it portrays the difficulties faced by a woman within prevailing social customs and relationships.

It is an important example of Gujarati cinema's engagement with the experiences of rural women.

Jesal Toral (1971)

The 1971 version of Jesal Toral was directed by Ravindra Dave. It drew upon the well-known folk narrative of Jesal and Toral and became an important landmark in the revival of Gujarati popular cinema during the 1970s.

The popularity of such films demonstrated the continuing appeal of Gujarat's folk legends and devotional traditions. The 1971 film should be distinguished from the earlier film adaptation of the same legend.

Bhavni Bhavai (1980)

Bhavni Bhavai, directed by Ketan Mehta, drew upon the Gujarati Bhavai theatrical tradition to address caste oppression and untouchability.

It received the National Film Award for Best Feature Film on National Integration for 1980. It is an important example of the relationship between regional folk culture, parallel cinema and social reform.

Expansion of Themes in Gujarati Cinema

Gujarati films have drawn upon several interconnected cultural and social subjects:

  • Devotional traditions: the lives and teachings of saints, as represented in Narsinh Mehta.
  • Literary heritage: adaptations of Gujarati literary works, such as Liludi Dharati and Kanku.
  • Folklore: popular regional legends, such as Jesal Toral.
  • Social reform: challenges to caste discrimination, gender inequality and restrictive customs.
  • Contemporary society: urban lifestyles, education, family relationships and changing aspirations.

The development of Gujarati cinema therefore involves both the preservation of inherited cultural traditions and the representation of changing social conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta (1932): Nanubhai Vakil; first Gujarati talkie.
  • Liludi Dharati (1968): Vallabh Choksi; Gujarati colour-film milestone.
  • Liludi Dharati: based on the novel by Chunilal Madia.
  • Kanku (1969): Kantilal Rathod; Pannalal Patel.
  • Jesal Toral (1971): Ravindra Dave.
  • Bhavni Bhavai (1980): Ketan Mehta; National Integration award.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries on Narsinh Mehta, Liludi Dharati, Kanku, Jesal Toral and Gujarati cinema; Hasmukh Baradi, Gujarati Cinema: Yesterday and Today, Yojana, August 1995; Directorate of Film Festivals, 31st National Film Festival catalogue, June 1984, Retrospective: National Integration award winners, 1965-1982; GKToday, Liludi Dharati milestone. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026. The project Volume 09 GCERT chapters could not be read from the available scans; the cited historical references are used instead.]

title: Development of Gujarati Cinema and Its Major Milestones

body:
National Film Awards

The Government of India instituted the National Film Awards in 1954 to recognise outstanding contributions to Indian cinema. The first edition honoured films of 1953.

The Marathi film Shyamchi Aai received the President's Gold Medal for Best All-India Feature Film at the first edition.

The National Film Awards recognise films from different linguistic and cultural traditions. Their purpose includes encouraging artistic excellence, socially relevant filmmaking and appreciation of India's regional diversity.

The awards are associated with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. They are administered through the National Film Development Corporation following the merger of the Directorate of Film Festivals into it in 2022.

Dadasaheb Phalke Award

The Dadasaheb Phalke Award is the Government of India's highest honour in the field of Indian cinema. It recognises an individual's outstanding contribution to the growth and development of Indian cinema over the course of a career.

  • Instituted: 1969.
  • Named after: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, the Father of Indian Cinema.
  • First recipient: Devika Rani.
  • Nature: lifetime contribution to Indian cinema.
  • Recognition: includes the Swarna Kamal, meaning Golden Lotus.

The award is not restricted to actors, directors or filmmakers working in Hindi cinema. Its scope extends across the Indian film industry.

Distinguishing the Principal Awards

The Dadasaheb Phalke Award honours an individual's lifetime contribution. The Best Feature Film award recognises an outstanding individual film across eligible Indian languages. A language-specific award, such as Best Gujarati Film, recognises a film within that linguistic category.

The official Dadasaheb Phalke Award must also be distinguished from privately organised film awards and festivals that use the name of Dadasaheb Phalke.

Gujarati Films Recognised at the National Level

Bhavni Bhavai

Ketan Mehta's Bhavni Bhavai received the National Film Award for Best Feature Film on National Integration for 1980. Its subject was caste discrimination and social inequality.

Hellaro

Hellaro, directed by Abhishek Shah, became the first Gujarati film to receive the National Film Award for Best Feature Film across Indian languages.

The award was announced on 9 August 2019 at the 66th National Film Awards, which covered films of 2018. The film received the Swarna Kamal, and its ensemble of 13 actresses received a Special Jury Award, shared in that category with another awardee.

Set in rural Kutch, Hellaro portrays women challenging patriarchal restrictions through Garba and collective self-expression.

Reva

At the same 66th National Film Awards, Reva, directed by Rahul Bhole and Vinit Kanojia, received the Best Gujarati Film award. It follows a spiritual journey associated with the Narmada.

A distinction between two awards

At the 66th National Film Awards, Hellaro received the all-India Best Feature Film award, whereas Reva received the language-specific Best Gujarati Film award. Both were honoured in the same edition.

Chhello Show

Chhello Show, also known as Last Film Show, was directed by Pan Nalin. It received the Best Gujarati Film award at the 69th National Film Awards for 2021, announced on 24 August 2023. Bhavin Rabari received the Best Child Artist award for the film.

72nd National Film Awards and Gujarat

As of the content cutoff of 26 November 2026, the 72nd National Film Awards had been presented at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), Gujarat, on 22 September 2026. This edition recognised films of 2024.

The winners had been announced on 18 July 2026. The Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 2024 was conferred on veteran actor Anant Nag during the September ceremony.

Maaran, directed by Abhishek Jain, received the Best Gujarati Film award in this edition.

The award year, announcement date and presentation date may differ. A question referring to a particular edition must therefore be answered using the corresponding award year and category.

Prelims focus

  • National Film Awards instituted in 1954 for films of 1953.
  • Dadasaheb Phalke Award instituted in 1969; first recipient Devika Rani.
  • Hellaro: first Gujarati film to win the all-India Best Feature Film award.
  • Reva: Best Gujarati Film at the 66th National Film Awards.
  • Chhello Show: Pan Nalin; Best Gujarati Film at the 69th edition.
  • 72nd edition: films of 2024; presented at Ekta Nagar on 22 September 2026.
